l: judgment on the wicked, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 65
s: The LORD says it is written before him that he will not keep silence but will repay into their bosom their own iniquities and their fathers' together. Those who forsake him are destined to the sword and bow down to the slaughter, because they did not answer when called and chose what he did not delight in. They will hunger, thirst, be disappointed, cry for sorrow and wail for anguish of spirit, and the Lord GOD will kill them.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 66
s: The LORD declares that heaven is his throne and earth his footstool, and that he looks to the poor and contrite who tremble at his word, while rejecting the sacrifices of those who choose their own ways and delight in abominations. He promises that Zion will give birth to her children suddenly and that Jerusalem will be a source of comfort, peace, and glory, with the LORD comforting his people like a mother. The LORD will come with fire, whirlwind, and sword to execute judgment on all flesh, especially those who practice idolatrous rites and eat pig's meat, the mouse, and abominable things. He will gather all nations to see his glory, send survivors to distant nations such as Tarshish, Pul, Lud, Tubal, and Javan to declare it, and bring back the brothers of his people to Jerusalem, selecting priests and Levites among them. The chapter closes with the promise that his people's offspring and name will endure like the new heavens and new earth, that all flesh will worship before him, and that they will look on the corpses of transgressors, whose worm and fire never end.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 66
s: The LORD declares heaven his throne and earth his footstool, and says he looks to the poor, contrite, and trembling. He rejects the sacrifices of those who choose their own ways, chooses their delusions, and will come with fire and sword to judge all flesh. He promises to comfort his people like a mother, gather all nations to see his glory, select priests and Levites, and make his people's name endure.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 66
s: Jerusalem is called to be rejoiced with by those who love her and mourn for her, and is pictured as a mother whose breasts comfort and satisfy. The LORD will extend peace to her like a river and the glory of the nations like an overflowing stream, and his people will be comforted in her. Her holy mountain is where the brothers from the nations are brought as an offering, and where all flesh will come to worship from one new moon and Sabbath to another.

l: those who tremble at the LORD's word, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 66
s: They are the poor and contrite ones to whom the LORD says he will look, and they are addressed as having brothers who hate them and cast them out for the LORD's name. Those brothers' mockery will end in their own disappointment. The trembling ones will see the LORD's comfort, rejoice, flourish like tender grass, and know the LORD's hand among his servants.

l: the adversaries and enemies of the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 66
s: The LORD's enemies are repaid what they deserve by a voice from the city and the temple, and he has indignation against them. He will come with fire, whirlwind chariots, and flames of rebuke, and those slain by him will be many. In the end their dead bodies are looked on, their worm does not die and their fire is not quenched, and they are loathsome to all mankind.

l: idolatrous worshippers (who choose their own ways), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 66
s: Their sacrifices are likened by the LORD to killing a man, breaking a dog's neck, offering pig's blood, and blessing an idol, because they chose their own ways and delight in abominations. The LORD will choose their delusions and bring their fears on them, since they did not answer or listen when he called. Those who sanctify themselves to go to the gardens and eat pig's meat, abominable things, and the mouse will come to an end together.

l: nations, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 66
s: The LORD will gather all nations and languages to see his glory. He will send survivors to Tarshish, Pul, Lud, Tubal, Javan, and far-away islands that have not heard his fame, and they will declare his glory among the nations. From all the nations the brothers of his people are brought to Jerusalem as an offering, and the glory of the nations flows to Jerusalem like an overflowing stream.

l: birth of Zion's children, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 66
s: Zion is described as giving birth before she travailed and delivering a son before her pain came, so that a land or nation is born in one day. The LORD asks whether he who brings to birth would shut the womb, affirming he will not. The birth leads into the invitation to nurse, be satisfied, and be comforted in Jerusalem.

l: judgment by fire, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 66
s: The LORD will come with fire and whirlwind-like chariots to give his anger with fierceness and his rebuke with flames. He will execute judgment by fire and by his sword on all flesh, with many slain. The fire is also pictured as unquenchable for the transgressors whose dead bodies are seen, and those who practice abominable rites come to an end together.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 1
s: Chapter 1 introduces Jeremiah, son of Hilkiah, a priest from Anathoth in Benjamin, whose prophetic ministry spans the reigns of Josiah, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah until Jerusalem's captivity in the fifth month. The LORD tells Jeremiah that he knew and sanctified him before birth and appointed him a prophet to the nations. Jeremiah protests that he is a child who cannot speak, but the LORD commands him to go where sent, touches his mouth, and puts his words there, setting him over nations and kingdoms to uproot, tear down, destroy, overthrow, build, and plant. Through the visions of an almond branch and a boiling cauldron tipping from the north, the LORD declares he watches over his word and will bring evil from the north on the inhabitants of the land. The LORD says he will call the northern kingdoms to besiege Jerusalem and Judah's cities because of idolatry, and he makes Jeremiah a fortified city, iron pillar, and bronze walls, promising that his opponents will fight him but not prevail.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 1
s: Jeremiah, son of Hilkiah and one of the priests in Anathoth in Benjamin, receives the LORD's word during the reigns of Josiah, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah. He objects that he is a child who cannot speak, but is touched on the mouth, given the LORD's words, and sent out. He sees an almond branch and a boiling cauldron, and is told to gird himself and speak without dismay.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 1
s: The LORD speaks to Jeremiah, declaring that he knew and sanctified him before birth, and appoints him a prophet to the nations. He touches Jeremiah's mouth, puts his words there, and promises to be with him and rescue him. He states that he watches over his word to perform it, and announces that he will call the northern kingdoms to bring evil on the land and will utter judgments for the people's idolatry.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 1
s: Judah is the realm whose kings Josiah, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah reigned during Jeremiah's ministry. Its cities are to be attacked by the northern kingdoms. Its kings, princes, priests, and people are the ones against whom Jeremiah is made a fortified city, iron pillar, and bronze walls.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 1
s: Jerusalem is named as being carried away captive in the fifth month, marking the end of the period of Jeremiah's word. The LORD says the northern families will set their thrones at the entrance of its gates and against all its walls around.

l: kingdoms of the north, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 1
s: The LORD says he will call all the families of the northern kingdoms, whom Jeremiah's vision of a boiling cauldron tipping from the north foreshadows. They will come and set their thrones at Jerusalem's gates, against its walls, and against all Judah's cities, as the means by which evil breaks out on the land.

l: inhabitants of the land (Judah), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 1
s: The LORD says evil will break out from the north on all the inhabitants of the land. They are charged with forsaking him, burning incense to other gods, and worshiping the works of their own hands. The people of the land are among those who will fight Jeremiah but not prevail.

l: Jeremiah's prophetic calling, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 1
s: Jeremiah's calling is described as predating his birth: the LORD knew and sanctified him and appointed him a prophet to the nations. Despite his protest of being a child, he is commissioned to go wherever sent and say whatever he is commanded, and is set over nations and kingdoms to uproot, tear down, destroy, overthrow, build, and plant. The LORD promises to be with him and rescue him, making him a fortified city, iron pillar, and bronze walls.

l: judgment on Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 1
s: The LORD announces judgment in the form of evil coming from the north, with the northern kingdoms besieging Jerusalem and the cities of Judah. The stated cause is that the people have forsaken him, burned incense to other gods, and worshiped the works of their own hands. The LORD says he will utter his judgments against them for all their wickedness.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 2
s: In Jeremiah 2 the LORD sends a message to Jerusalem, the house of Jacob, and Israel, recalling Israel's early devotion as a bride in the wilderness and holiness to him. He charges that the fathers, priests, law-handlers, rulers, and prophets abandoned him for Baal and worthless things, trading their glory for what doesn't profit. He says his people committed two evils: forsaking him, the spring of living waters, and digging broken cisterns. Israel has suffered ruin and captivity, yet seeks help from Egypt and Assyria, and denies guilt while pursuing idols under every green tree. The LORD announces he will contend and judge them, saying the gods they trust cannot save them and that they will be ashamed of Egypt as they were of Assyria.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 2
s: The LORD recalls Israel's youthful kindness and love, and accuses the people, their leaders, and their fathers of forsaking him, the spring of living waters, though he brought them out of Egypt and into a plentiful land. He declares he will contend with them and their children's children, and will judge them for claiming innocence. He has rejected those in whom they trust and challenges their gods to save them.

l: Israel, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 2
s: Israel is remembered as holiness to the LORD and first fruits of his increase, who followed him in the wilderness as a bride. Having defiled the land, followed Baal, forsaken the LORD, and sought help from Egypt and Assyria, it has become a captive whose land and cities are laid waste. It denies guilt and is told it will be ashamed and leave with hands on its head.

l: Egypt, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 2
s: Egypt is named as the land the LORD brought Israel out of, and its Memphis and Tahpanhes are said to have broken the crown of Israel's head. Israel goes there to drink the waters of the Shihor, seeking help. The LORD says Israel will be ashamed of Egypt, as it was of Assyria.

l: Assyria, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 2
s: Assyria is a place Israel turns to, going to drink the waters of the River instead of trusting the LORD. The LORD says Israel was already ashamed of Assyria and will likewise be ashamed of Egypt.

l: Baal, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 2
s: Baal is the god by whom the prophets prophesied, following things that do not profit. Israel denies having gone after the Baals, but the LORD tells it to look at its way in the valley and know what it has done.

l: other gods, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 2
s: The LORD calls them no gods, noting that no nation changes its gods, yet his people exchanged their glory for what doesn't profit. Israel tells wood 'You are my father' and a stone 'You have given birth to me', and Judah has as many gods as towns. The LORD challenges them to arise and save in the time of trouble.

l: Israel's unfaithfulness and idolatry, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 2
s: The LORD describes it as forsaking him for broken cisterns, bowing on every high hill and under every green tree like a prostitute, and breaking the yoke saying 'I will not serve'. He compares Israel to a noble vine turned degenerate, to a swift dromedary and a wild donkey in heat, and says its iniquity cannot be washed away. The sin includes innocent blood in its skirts, claims of innocence, and forgetting the LORD for days without number.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 3
s: In Chapter 3, the LORD appeals to unfaithful Israel and Judah using the image of a divorced wife who has gone to other men, accusing the people of polluting the land with prostitution and wickedness. In the days of King Josiah, the LORD recounts that backsliding Israel committed adultery on every high mountain and under every green tree and was given a certificate of divorce, yet treacherous Judah saw this and also played the prostitute, returning only in pretense. The LORD commands a proclamation toward the north inviting Israel to return, acknowledge her iniquity, and receive mercy, promising to bring a remnant to Zion, give shepherds after his heart, and call Jerusalem 'The LORD's Throne' where all nations gather. He foresees Judah and Israel walking together out of the north to the inherited land. The chapter closes with a voice on the bare heights weeping and confessing, as the people admit that salvation is in the LORD alone and lie down in shame for sinning from their youth.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 3
s: The LORD calls backsliding Israel and Judah to return, declaring that he is merciful, will not keep anger forever, and is a husband to them. He recounts having divorced Israel, promises to heal their backsliding, give shepherds after his heart, and bring a remnant to Zion. He expresses his desire to treat them as children who would call him 'My Father'.

l: Israel, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 3
s: Backsliding Israel is said to have played the prostitute on every high mountain and under every green tree and did not return, so the LORD put her away with a certificate of divorce. She is nevertheless called to return and acknowledge her iniquity, and is judged more righteous than treacherous Judah. Her children are portrayed weeping on the bare heights and confessing their sin, shame, and disobedience from their youth.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 3
s: Judah is called Israel's treacherous sister, who saw Israel's divorce yet had no fear and also played the prostitute. She has not returned to the LORD with her whole heart, only in pretense, and is judged less righteous than Israel. The LORD promises that in those days the house of Judah will walk with the house of Israel and come together out of the north to the inherited land.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 3
s: The LORD promises that Jerusalem will be called 'The LORD's Throne' and that all nations will gather to it in his name. In that time the ark of the covenant will no longer be remembered or missed, and the people will no longer follow the stubbornness of their evil hearts. Zion is the place to which the LORD will bring his returning people.

l: Israel's idolatry and unfaithfulness, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 3
s: The people's unfaithfulness is depicted as prostitution and adultery with many lovers, on high mountains and under green trees, and with stones and wood, which polluted the land. Its consequences include withheld showers and no latter rain, and Israel's refusal to be ashamed. The people finally confess that shame has devoured their fathers' labor, flocks, herds, sons, and daughters, and that they have not obeyed the LORD's voice.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 4
s: In this chapter the LORD calls Israel to return to him and put away abominations, and urges the men of Judah and Jerusalem to break up fallow ground and circumcise their hearts lest his wrath burn like fire. He announces evil and great destruction coming from the north, described as a lion and destroyer of nations, and the people are told to blow the trumpet, flee to fortified cities, and mourn in sackcloth. The prophet protests that the people were deceived with promises of peace, laments his anguish at the sound of war, and sees a vision of the earth returned to waste and void. The LORD declares the people foolish and skilled at evil, says the land will be desolate though he will not make a full end, and that he will not relent. Jerusalem, pictured as a woman adorning herself in vain, is despised by her lovers and cries out like a woman in labor before murderers.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 4
s: The LORD calls Israel to return and put away abominations, promising they will not be removed if they do. He warns Judah and Jerusalem of fiery wrath, announces evil from the north, and declares that the people are foolish and have brought this on themselves by their wickedness. He states that the whole land will be desolate yet he will not make a full end, and that he has planned it and will not repent or turn back.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 4
s: Judah is addressed with a call to break up fallow ground, circumcise their hearts, and sound the alarm, and it is warned that watchers from a far country will raise their voice against its cities. Its land is to be made desolate, with cities laid waste and forsaken, though the LORD says he will not make a full end.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 4
s: Jerusalem is told to wash its heart from wickedness so it may be saved, and is asked how long its evil thoughts will lodge within. It is besieged all around like a field by keepers because of its rebellion, and is pictured as a woman who adorns herself in vain, despised by her lovers who seek her life. The daughter of Zion cries out like a woman in labor, fainting before murderers.

l: destroyer (the lion from the north), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 4
s: A lion, a destroyer of nations, has gone up from his thicket and is on his way from his place to make the land desolate and lay its cities waste without inhabitant. He is described as coming up like clouds, with chariots like a whirlwind and horses swifter than eagles.

l: overflowing waters from the north, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 4
s: The LORD says he will bring evil and great destruction from the north, signaled by a standard toward Zion and the trumpet. Its effects include a hot wind that does not cleanse, destruction on destruction, the land laid waste, tents destroyed, and cities fleeing. The prophet sees the earth waste and void, mountains trembling, no man, birds fled, and the fruitful field a wilderness.

l: people of Judah and Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 4
s: The people are told to circumcise their hearts, flee to fortified cities, and lament in sackcloth, since the LORD's fierce anger has not turned back. The LORD calls them foolish children who do not know him, skillful in evil but not in doing good. At that day the hearts of the king and princes will perish, and priests and prophets will be astonished.

l: speaker (the prophet), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 4
s: The speaker protests to the Lord GOD that the people were greatly deceived by promises of peace while the sword reaches the heart. He expresses deep anguish, a trembling heart, and distress at the trumpet and the alarm of war, asking how long he must see the standard. He relates a series of visions of the earth devastated, and hears the voice of the daughter of Zion in travail.

l: wickedness and idolatry, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 4
s: The LORD calls for abominations to be put away from his sight and for evil thoughts to be washed from the heart. He says the people's way and doings have brought the coming disaster, and that their wickedness is bitter and reaches their heart. Their rebellion against him is given as the reason for the besieging watchers and the coming desolation.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 5
s: In Chapter 5, the LORD sends a search through the streets of Jerusalem for a single just person who seeks truth, and finds the people, both poor and great, have refused correction, sworn falsely, and broken the yoke. The LORD declares that the houses of Israel and Judah have acted treacherously, committing adultery, denying him, and trusting in false prophets who say no evil will come. He announces judgment: a lion, wolf, and leopard, and then a mighty, ancient nation of unknown language that will devour harvests, flocks, and fortified cities. Even so, he promises not to make a full end of them, and says that as they served foreign gods in their land, they will serve strangers in a land not theirs. The chapter closes by condemning wicked men who trap others and grow rich through deceit while ignoring the fatherless and needy, and by lamenting that prophets prophesy falsely, priests rule by their own authority, and the people love it so.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 5
s: The LORD challenges anyone to find one just person in Jerusalem and says he would pardon the city if so. He accuses Israel and Judah of treachery, swearing falsely, adultery, and idolatry, and announces punishment by wild beasts and a foreign nation while promising not to make a full end. He presents himself as the one who set the sea's bounds and gives rain and harvest, and asks whether he should not be avenged on such a nation.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 5
s: Jerusalem is the city whose streets and wide places are searched for a single man who does justly and seeks truth. Its walls are to be gone up on and destroyed, though not completely, and it is said that its people swear falsely even while saying 'As the LORD lives.'

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 5
s: The people are shown as stubborn: stricken but not grieved, refusing correction, with faces harder than rock, and having broken the yoke and burst the bonds. They have forsaken the LORD, sworn by no-gods, denied that evil will come, and have a revolting and rebellious heart that does not fear him. They are told they will lose their harvest and serve strangers in a foreign land, and that their sins have withheld good from them.

l: prophets, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 5
s: The prophets are said to become wind, with the word not in them, and the LORD says he will make his words in Jeremiah's mouth a fire against the people. The chapter ends by stating that the prophets prophesy falsely, the priests rule by their own authority, and the people love it so.

l: wicked men, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 5
s: Wicked men are found among the LORD's people, lying in wait like fowlers, setting traps and catching men. Their houses are full of deceit like a cage full of birds, and through it they have become great, rich, fat, and shining. They do not plead the cause of the fatherless or defend the rights of the needy, and the LORD asks whether he should not punish for this.

l: nation from far away (invader against Israel), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 5
s: The LORD says he will bring a mighty, ancient nation from far away on the house of Israel, whose language they do not know or understand. Its quiver is an open tomb and all its people are mighty men. It will eat up the harvest, bread, sons' and daughters' food, flocks, herds, vines, and fig trees, and beat down the fortified cities with the sword.

l: divine punishment and exile, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 5
s: Punishment is announced through a lion, wolf, and leopard, through words that become fire devouring the people as wood, and through a foreign invasion. The LORD limits it by promising not to make a full end, and says that because the people served foreign gods in their land, they will serve strangers in a land that is not theirs.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 6
s: Chapter 6 warns the children of Benjamin to flee Jerusalem because evil is coming from the north. The LORD of Armies commands that trees be cut down and a siege mound built against Jerusalem, the city to be visited because it is filled with oppression, violence, and wickedness. The speaker laments that the people's ears are uncircumcised, that prophets and priests deal falsely and cry 'Peace, peace!' when there is no peace, and that the people refused the good old paths and the watchmen's trumpet. The LORD declares their offerings unacceptable and describes a cruel people from the north, armed with bow and spear and riding horses, who will come against the daughter of Zion. The chapter ends with the people mourning in terror and the LORD calling them rejected silver, since refining cannot remove their wickedness.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 6
s: Jerusalem is called to flee from and is named the city to be visited, with a mound to be cast up against it because it is filled with oppression. It is urged to be instructed lest the LORD make it a desolation and an uninhabited land. It is addressed as the daughter of Zion, whom a northern people will attack and whose palaces will be destroyed.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 6
s: The LORD of Armies commands the cutting down of trees and the building of a siege mound against Jerusalem, and declares He will stretch out His hand on the inhabitants. He rejects their burnt offerings and sacrifices, sets stumbling blocks before them, and offers the old paths that bring rest, which they refuse. He finally calls the people rejected silver because He has rejected them.

l: northern invaders, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 6
s: A people and great nation stirred up from the uttermost parts of the earth comes from the north against the daughter of Zion. They hold bow and spear, are cruel and merciless, roar like the sea, and ride horses in array. Their report makes the people's hands feeble and brings anguish like a woman in labor.

l: people of Judah (Jerusalem's inhabitants), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 6
s: The people, from least to greatest and from prophet to priest, are given to covetousness and false dealing, and they heal the people's hurt superficially, crying 'Peace, peace!' They feel no shame, refuse the good way and the watchmen's trumpet, and reject the LORD's word and law. Their houses, fields, and wives will be turned to others, and old and young alike will be taken, while they are called bronze, iron, and rejected silver.

l: coming destruction, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 6
s: Destruction looks out from the north, with siege against Jerusalem, the cutting off of the daughter of Zion, and the ruin of her palaces. It will fall on children, young men, husbands, wives, and the aged, and on fathers, sons, neighbors, and friends. The people respond with terror, sackcloth, and ashes, mourning as for an only son, since the destroyer will suddenly come.

l: wickedness and oppression, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 6
s: Jerusalem produces wickedness as a well produces water, and violence and destruction are heard in her, with sickness and wounds ever before the LORD. Covetousness, falsehood, slander, and shamelessness mark everyone from least to greatest. The refining process is in vain because the wicked are not plucked away, which is why the LORD brings evil as the fruit of their thoughts.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 7
s: The LORD commands Jeremiah to stand at the gate of the LORD's house and tell the people of Judah to amend their ways rather than trust in the slogan 'the LORD's temple.' The LORD condemns their theft, murder, adultery, false swearing, and worship of Baal and other gods, calls the temple a den of robbers, and warns that he will treat it as he treated Shiloh. He forbids Jeremiah to intercede for the people, denounces their cakes for the queen of the sky and their rejection of the prophets, and says they have done worse than their fathers. The chapter ends with the abomination of Topheth, where children are burned, and with the prediction that it will become the valley of Slaughter, the dead will be unburied food for birds and animals, and the land will become a waste with all joy silenced.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 7
s: The LORD sends Jeremiah to the temple gate, demands that Judah amend its ways and execute justice, and promises they can stay in the land if they do. He rejects their trust in the temple, says he has seen their wickedness, forbids Jeremiah to pray for them, and declares that his anger will be poured out on the place, with the land becoming a waste. He says he never commanded burnt offerings as such, but commanded obedience to his voice, and that he never commanded or thought of burning children at Topheth.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 7
s: Jeremiah receives the LORD's word and is told to stand in the gate of the LORD's house and proclaim it to all Judah entering to worship. He is told not to pray or intercede for the people because the LORD will not hear, and is warned that the people will neither listen nor answer him when he speaks and calls to them. He is also told to tell them that truth has perished and to take up a lamentation.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 7
s: The people of Judah are accused of trusting lying words, stealing, murdering, committing adultery, swearing falsely, burning incense to Baal, and following other gods. Families make cakes for the queen of the sky, and the children of Judah set abominations in the temple and burn their sons and daughters at Topheth. They have not listened to the prophets, have stiffened their necks, and have done worse than their fathers. The LORD announces that he will cast them out as he did Ephraim's offspring and that their cities will lose all mirth and gladness.

l: the LORD’s house, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 7
s: The temple, called by the LORD's name, is the place where Jeremiah must proclaim his message and where the people come to say 'We are delivered.' The LORD asks whether it has become a den of robbers and says the people have set abominations in it to defile it. He announces that he will do to it as he did to Shiloh.

l: Shiloh, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 7
s: Shiloh is the place where the LORD caused his name to dwell at the first. The people are told to go and see what he did to it because of the wickedness of his people Israel, and it serves as the pattern for what he will do to the temple in Jerusalem.

l: Topheth, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 7
s: Topheth, in the valley of the son of Hinnom, is where the people of Judah built high places to burn their sons and daughters in the fire, which the LORD says he did not command and which never came into his mind. He declares it will be renamed the valley of Slaughter, where they will bury the dead until there is no more room.

l: coming judgment and desolation, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 7
s: The LORD announces that his anger and wrath will be poured out on this place, on man, animal, trees, and the fruit of the ground, burning without being quenched. He says he will cast Judah out of his sight, leave corpses as food for birds and animals with no one to frighten them away, and end the voices of mirth, gladness, bridegroom, and bride in Judah's cities and Jerusalem's streets, as the land becomes a waste.

l: false trust in the temple, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 7
s: The people repeat the phrase 'The LORD's temple, the LORD's temple, the LORD's temple' as lying words that cannot profit them. The LORD says they continue in theft, murder, adultery, and idolatry and then stand before him in his house saying 'We are delivered,' so that they may keep doing abominations. He rejects this trust and says real dwelling in the land depends on amended ways and justice.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 8
s: Chapter 8 records the LORD's judgment on the people of Jerusalem and Judah for persistent backsliding and deceit. The bones of kings, princes, priests, prophets, and inhabitants will be dug from their graves and spread before the sun, moon, and army of the sky they worshiped, and survivors in exile will prefer death to life. The LORD contrasts his people's refusal to return with the stork, turtledove, swallow, and crane that know their seasons, and condemns the scribes' false pen, the wise men, and the prophets and priests who cry 'Peace, peace' when there is no peace. An invading enemy, heard from Dan with snorting horses, will devour the land, and the LORD will send unchARMable serpents among them. The speaker laments the people's hurt and asks why there is no healing when there is balm and a physician in Gilead.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 8
s: The LORD announces that the bones of Judah's dead will be exposed and that survivors will choose death over life. He accuses the people of refusing to return, promises to consume them and send unchARMable serpents, and is heard complaining that they provoked him with engraved images and foreign idols.

l: people of Judah and Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 8
s: The people of Jerusalem are charged with perpetual backsliding, clinging to deceit, covetousness, and shamelessness, and with not knowing the LORD's law, unlike the migrating birds that know their times. Their wives and fields will be given to others, their harvest will fail, and they lament that they looked for peace and found dismay.

l: bones of the dead, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 8
s: The bones of the kings of Judah, princes, priests, prophets, and inhabitants of Jerusalem will be brought out of their graves and spread before the sun, moon, and army of the sky. They will not be gathered or buried and will lie like dung on the surface of the earth.

l: sun, moon, and army of the sky, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 8
s: The sun, moon, and army of the sky are the objects the people have loved, served, followed, sought, and worshiped. Before them the bones of the dead will be laid out, showing the worship's futility.

l: invading enemy, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 8
s: An unnamed enemy is heard from Dan, with the snorting of horses and neighing of strong ones making the whole land tremble. They have come and devoured the land, the city, and all who dwell in it.

l: speaker lamenting, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 8
s: The speaker grieves that his heart is faint and that he is hurt, mourning and dismayed at the hurt of the daughter of his people. He asks whether there is no balm or physician in Gilead and why the people's health is not recovered.

l: backsliding and deceit, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 8
s: The people's perpetual backsliding is marked by clinging to deceit, refusing to repent, and rushing on their own course like a horse into battle. Deceit also appears in the scribes' false pen, in the prophets' and priests' false dealing, and in the empty cry of 'Peace, peace.'

l: judgment and destruction, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 8
s: Judgment takes the form of exposed bones, survivors preferring death, loss of wives and fields, and fruitless vines and fig trees. It also comes through an invading army, poisoned water, and serpents that cannot be charmed, and the people confess that the harvest is past and they are not saved.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 9
s: In Chapter 9 the speaker laments the slain of the daughter of his people and wishes to flee from a people he calls adulterers and treacherous men. The LORD describes a society full of lies, slander, and betrayal among neighbors and brothers, who refuse to know him, and he declares he will melt and test them and punish them. He announces that Jerusalem will become heaps and the cities of Judah a desolation, because the people forsook his law and followed their own stubbornness and the Baals. He promises wormwood, poisoned water, scattering among the nations, and the sword, and calls for mourning women to wail as death enters windows and palaces. The chapter closes by saying that the wise, mighty, and rich should not glory in those things but in knowing the LORD, who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, and by announcing punishment on Egypt, Judah, Edom, Ammon, Moab, and all Israel, who are uncircumcised in flesh or heart.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 9
s: The LORD accuses the people of deceit, forsaking his law, and following the Baals, and he vows to melt and test them, feed them wormwood and poisoned water, scatter them among the nations, and send the sword. He makes Jerusalem heaps and Judah a desolation, and he declares that he exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness and delights in these. He also announces punishment on all the nations and on Israel as uncircumcised in flesh or heart.

l: the daughter of my people, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 9
s: The speaker wishes to weep day and night for her slain. The LORD asks how he should deal with her, and he says he will melt and test the people.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 9
s: The unnamed speaker laments with tears for the slain of his people and wishes to leave them for a wilderness lodging, since they are adulterers and treacherous. He also asks who is wise enough to understand why the land has perished, and he relays the LORD's word, urging the women to teach lamentation. The name Jeremiah does not appear in this chapter.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 9
s: The LORD declares he will make Jerusalem heaps and a dwelling place of jackals. A wailing is heard out of Zion because of ruin and cast-down dwellings.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 9
s: The LORD says he will make the cities of Judah a desolation without inhabitant. Judah is also listed among the nations to be punished as uncircumcised in flesh.

l: deceit and treachery, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 9
s: The people bend their tongues like bows for falsehood, and brothers supplant and neighbors slander. Friends deceive each other, and one speaks peaceably while plotting ambush in his heart. Through deceit they refuse to know the LORD, and this is a reason the LORD gives for punishing them.

l: coming judgment and desolation, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 9
s: The land is burned up and empty, with no one passing through, no livestock, and birds and animals fled. The LORD promises wormwood, poisoned water, scattering, and the sword, and death enters windows and palaces, with corpses lying like dung on the open field. The cause given is forsaking his law and following the Baals, and the punishment extends to the nations and to Israel.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 10
s: The LORD addresses the house of Israel, warning them not to learn the ways of the nations or fear the signs of the sky, since the nations' idols are only wood decked with silver and gold, unable to speak, move, do good or do evil. In contrast, the LORD is the true, living God and everlasting King, who made the earth by his power and controls the weather, and the gods who did not make the heavens and earth will perish. The text then turns to the people under siege, who are told to gather their wares because the LORD will sling out the inhabitants of the land. A lamenting voice mourns a serious wound, a destroyed tent, and lost children, blaming the shepherds who did not inquire of the LORD, and announces news of a commotion from the north that will make Judah's cities a desolation. The speaker admits that man cannot direct his own steps, asks the LORD to correct him gently, and asks that wrath be poured out on the nations that devoured Jacob.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 10
s: The LORD is declared incomparable, the true and living God and everlasting King, who made the earth by his power, established the world by his wisdom, and stretched out the heavens. He makes the earth tremble at his wrath, and says he will sling out the inhabitants of the land and distress them. The speaker asks him to correct gently and to pour out wrath on the nations that devoured Jacob.

l: Israel, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 10
s: The house of Israel is called to hear the LORD's word and is told not to learn the way of the nations or be dismayed at the signs of the sky. Jacob's portion is said to be unlike the idols, since the LORD of Armies, maker of all things, is his name and Israel is the tribe of his inheritance.

l: nations, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 10
s: The nations are dismayed at the signs of the sky and follow customs the text calls vanity. Their wise men and kings are said to have no one like the LORD, and they are called brutish and foolish for being instructed by idols. They are also accused of devouring Jacob, consuming him and laying waste his habitation, and the speaker asks that the LORD's wrath be poured out on them because they do not know him or call on his name.

l: idols, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 10
s: Idols are described as wood cut from the forest, worked by an ax, decked with silver from Tarshish and gold from Uphaz, clothed in blue and purple, and fastened with nails so they cannot move. They cannot speak, do evil, or do good, have no breath, and are falsehood and delusion. The text says they will perish in the time of their visitation, as will the gods that did not make the heavens and the earth.

l: inhabitants of the land, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 10
s: The inhabitants of the land, described as living under siege, are told to gather up their wares out of the land. The LORD says he will sling them out at this time and distress them so that they feel it.

l: speaker (lamenting voice), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 10
s: The speaker cries out over a serious wound, a destroyed tent, broken cords, and children who are gone, with no one left to set up the curtains. He says he must bear his grief, acknowledges that a man's way is not in himself, and asks the LORD to correct him gently and not in anger lest he be reduced to nothing.

l: coming destruction, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 10
s: News is announced of a great commotion coming out of the north country. It is said to be aimed at making the cities of Judah a desolation and a dwelling place of jackals.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 11
s: The LORD commands Jeremiah to proclaim the words of the covenant to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, recalling the covenant made with their fathers when he brought them out of Egypt. Because Judah and Israel broke it by following other gods and Baal, the LORD announces unavoidable evil, forbids Jeremiah to pray for the people, and says their gods will not save them. Jeremiah learns that people are plotting to kill him and, likening himself to a gentle lamb led to slaughter, entrusts his cause to the LORD. The LORD answers by pronouncing punishment on the men of Anathoth who seek Jeremiah's life, saying their young men will die by the sword, their children by famine, and no remnant will remain.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 11
s: The LORD commands Jeremiah to proclaim the covenant, recalls that he brought the fathers out of Egypt and protested to them repeatedly, and declares evil on Judah that he will not relent from or hear their cries about. He forbids Jeremiah to pray for the people, reveals the plot against Jeremiah to him, and pronounces punishment on the men of Anathoth, whom he will leave with no remnant.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 11
s: Jeremiah receives the word of the LORD, answers "Amen, LORD," and is told to proclaim the covenant in the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem. He is forbidden to pray for the people, learns of a plot against his life, describes himself as a gentle lamb led to slaughter, and entrusts his cause to the LORD, expecting to see vengeance on his enemies.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 11
s: The men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem are addressed with the covenant words and are accused of a conspiracy, of returning to the iniquities of their forefathers, and of serving other gods. They have set up as many gods as they have cities and altars to Baal as they have streets, and the LORD will bring inescapable evil on them, ignoring their cries and leaving their gods unable to save them.

l: covenant (LORD's covenant with Judah), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 11
s: The covenant is the one the LORD commanded the fathers when he brought them out of Egypt: obey his voice so they would be his people and he their God, with the promised land flowing with milk and honey. Jeremiah is told to proclaim it, and its words are brought on the people because the house of Israel and the house of Judah have broken it.

l: Baal, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 11
s: Baal is the god to whom the people of Jerusalem and Judah burn incense on altars set up in every street. This offering provokes the LORD to anger and is named as a cause of the evil he pronounces against them.

l: men of Anathoth, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 11
s: The men of Anathoth seek Jeremiah's life and tell him not to prophesy in the LORD's name, or he will die by their hand. The LORD says he will punish them: the young men will die by the sword, their sons and daughters by famine, and no remnant will remain in the year of their visitation.

l: plot against Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 11
s: The LORD gives Jeremiah knowledge of a plan to destroy him, which he had not known, in which his enemies say they will destroy the tree with its fruit and cut him off from the land of the living so his name is remembered no more. Jeremiah brings his cause to the LORD, who responds by pronouncing punishment on the men of Anathoth who seek his life.

l: judgment on Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 11
s: The LORD declares he will bring evil on Judah and Jerusalem that they cannot escape, and he will not listen when they cry to him. Their gods will not save them, and the olive tree he planted and named beautiful is set on fire with its branches broken because of the evil of Israel and Judah in offering incense to Baal.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 12
s: In Chapter 12 a speaker complains to the LORD that the wicked prosper and are at ease, honoring God with their mouths but not their hearts, and asks that they be pulled out like sheep for slaughter. He also asks how long the land will mourn. The LORD answers that the speaker must prepare for harder trials, since even his brothers and his father's house have betrayed him. The LORD then laments that he has forsaken his house and given his beloved heritage to her enemies, so that many shepherds have made his vineyard a desolate wilderness. Finally the LORD declares he will pluck up his evil neighbors who touch Israel's inheritance and then have compassion on them, restoring them if they learn to swear by his name, but destroying any nation that will not listen.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 12
s: The LORD is addressed as righteous and as one who knows and tests the speaker's heart. He answers the complaint by warning of harder trials and by lamenting that he has forsaken his house and given his beloved heritage to her enemies. He declares he will pluck up the evil neighbors, then have compassion and restore them if they learn his ways, but destroy any nation that refuses to listen.

l: the wicked, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 12
s: The wicked are described as planted and rooted by the LORD, growing and bearing fruit, with God near in their mouth but far from their heart. They say 'He won't see our latter end,' and the speaker asks that they be pulled out like sheep for slaughter.

l: speaker (the complainant to the LORD), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 12
s: The speaker contends with the LORD, asking why the way of the wicked prospers, and says the LORD knows and tests his heart. The LORD replies that he has been wearied by footmen and cannot yet contend with horses, and that his brothers and father's house have dealt treacherously with him, so he should not believe their beautiful words.

l: heritage (the LORD's heritage), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 12
s: The LORD's heritage, his dearly beloved, has been cast off and given into the hand of her enemies. She has become to him like a lion in the forest that uttered her voice against him, and he says he hated her. She is also likened to a speckled bird of prey surrounded by birds of prey, with animals assembled to devour her, and to a vineyard trodden by many shepherds and made a desolate wilderness.

l: the land, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 12
s: The land mourns and its herbs wither because of the wickedness of its inhabitants, and the animals and birds are consumed. It is made wholly desolate because no one cares, and destroyers and the LORD's sword devour it from end to end so that no flesh has peace. The people have sown wheat and reaped thorns.

l: evil neighbors, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 12
s: The evil neighbors touch the inheritance the LORD gave Israel, and he says he will pluck them up from their land and pluck the house of Judah from among them. After that he will return and have compassion, bringing each back to his heritage and land. If they diligently learn his people's ways and swear by his name, as they once taught his people to swear by Baal, they will be built up among his people, but a nation that will not hear will be plucked up and destroyed.

l: Israel, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 12
s: Israel is the people whom the LORD caused to inherit the inheritance that the evil neighbors touch. The house of Judah is to be plucked up from among those neighbors, and the neighbors are told to learn the ways of the LORD's people.

l: the prosperity of the wicked, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 12
s: The speaker raises it as the central question: why the way of the wicked prospers and the treacherous are at ease. It is described as the LORD's own planting, with the wicked taking root, growing and bearing fruit, though only in word and not in heart. The speaker asks that they be pulled out for the day of slaughter, and the LORD's reply speaks of wheat sown yielding thorns and of fruits to be ashamed of.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 13
s: In Chapter 13 the LORD commands the narrator to buy a linen belt, wear it, and later hide it in a cleft of rock by the Euphrates. After many days he digs it up and finds it ruined and profitable for nothing. The LORD explains that this is how he will ruin the pride of Judah and Jerusalem, whose evil people refuse to hear him and follow other gods, though he had made Israel and Judah cling to him as a belt clings to a waist. The narrator is told to announce that all will be filled with drunkenness and dashed against one another without pity, and he urges the people to humble themselves before darkness comes. The chapter ends with the king and queen mother warned of lost crowns, Judah carried away captive from the north, and Jerusalem rebuked for its iniquity, abominations, and shame.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 13
s: The LORD commands the narrator to buy, wear, hide, and retrieve a linen belt, then explains that it represents the ruin of Judah's and Jerusalem's pride. He declares he will fill all the inhabitants, including kings, priests, and prophets, with drunkenness and dash them against one another without pity. He had caused Israel and Judah to cling to him for a people, a name, praise, and glory, but they would not hear.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 13
s: The narrator obeys the LORD's commands: he buys the belt, wears it, hides it by the Euphrates, and digs it up after many days to find it ruined. He is told to deliver the message about containers filled with wine and the coming drunkenness. He pleads with the people to hear and says his soul will weep in secret and his eye run down with tears because the LORD's flock has been taken captive.

l: linen belt (Jeremiah's belt), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 13
s: The linen belt is bought, worn on the waist without being put in water, then hidden in a cleft of the rock by the Euphrates. When retrieved after many days it is ruined and profitable for nothing. It symbolizes how the LORD will ruin Judah's pride and how the evil people will become profitable for nothing, and it also pictures how Israel and Judah were made to cling to him.

l: Euphrates, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 13
s: The Euphrates is the place where the narrator is sent to hide the belt in a cleft of the rock. He returns there after many days and digs up the ruined belt.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 13
s: Judah's pride is to be ruined as the belt was, and the whole house of Judah had been made to cling to the LORD but would not hear. Its cities of the South are shut up with no one to open them, and all of Judah is wholly carried away captive.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 13
s: Jerusalem's great pride is to be ruined, and all its inhabitants are to be filled with drunkenness. It is accused of abominations, adulteries, neighing, and lewdness on the hills. It is told it will not be made clean, and its skirts will be uncovered so that its shame appears, with the LORD asking how long it will yet be.

l: people of Judah and Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 13
s: This evil people refuse to hear the LORD's words, walk in the stubbornness of their heart, and go after other gods to serve and worship them. They will become like the ruined belt, profitable for nothing. They are likened to those who cannot change, as the Ethiopian cannot change his skin nor the leopard his spots, and they are to be scattered like stubble before the wind because they forgot the LORD and trusted in falsehood.

l: pride, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 13
s: Pride is the fault the LORD says he will ruin in Judah and Jerusalem, as shown by the ruined belt. The people are urged not to be proud and to give glory to the LORD, and the narrator weeps in secret for their pride. The king and queen mother are told to humble themselves because their crowns of glory have come down.

l: drunkenness and destruction (judgment), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 13
s: The LORD says every container should be filled with wine and applies this to filling the inhabitants of the land, including kings, priests, prophets, and all of Jerusalem, with drunkenness. He will dash fathers and sons against one another, without pity, sparing, or compassion. Further judgment includes darkness, scattering like stubble, and the exposure of Jerusalem's shame.

l: captivity, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 13
s: The narrator weeps because the LORD's flock has been taken captive. Judah is said to be carried away captive, all of them wholly, and the cities of the South are shut up. A foe is seen coming from the north, and the king and queen mother are asked where the beautiful flock given to them has gone.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 14
s: Chapter 14 opens with the LORD's word to Jeremiah concerning a drought that devastates Judah and Jerusalem: nobles' children find empty cisterns, plowmen cover their heads, and the doe and wild donkeys fail for lack of grass. The people confess their sins and plead for the LORD to act for his name's sake and not leave them, but the LORD says they have loved to wander and refuses to accept them, forbidding Jeremiah to pray for them. Jeremiah objects that the prophets promise assured peace, and the LORD answers that these prophets speak lies he never sent, and that they and their hearers will die by sword and famine. Jeremiah is told to weep for the slain and famine-stricken, and the chapter ends with a communal prayer acknowledging wickedness, asking the LORD not to break his covenant, and trusting him as the one who can send rain.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 14
s: The LORD sends word to Jeremiah about the drought and declares he does not accept the people because they have loved to wander, and will remember their iniquity and punish them. He forbids Jeremiah to pray for them, says he will not hear their fasts or accept their offerings, denies sending the prophets who promise peace, and vows to consume them by sword, famine, and pestilence. The people's closing prayer appeals to him as the God who made all things and alone can give rain.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 14
s: Jeremiah receives the LORD's word about the drought and is told not to pray for the people for their good. He protests that the prophets promise peace, and is told those prophets are liars. He is instructed to say a word of lament, with eyes running down with tears night and day over the broken people.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 14
s: Judah mourns and its gates languish as the drought strikes. The people sit in black on the ground and the land is cracked without rain. Judah is named in the people's prayer asking whether the LORD has utterly rejected it.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 14
s: The cry of Jerusalem goes up because of the drought. The LORD says those who heed the false prophets will be cast out in its streets, unburied, from famine and sword. In the prayer, the people ask whether the LORD has loathed Zion.

l: drought, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 14
s: The drought brings cracked ground, empty cisterns, disappointed plowmen, a doe forsaking her young, and wild donkeys panting with failing eyes for lack of vegetation. It is the occasion for the LORD's word to Jeremiah and the people's prayer. The chapter ends by affirming that only the LORD, not the vanities of the nations, can cause rain.

l: people of Judah and Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 14
s: The people suffer the drought, confess their sins, and plead for the LORD to act for his name's sake and not leave them. The LORD answers that they have loved to wander and not restrained their feet, so he does not accept them. They end by acknowledging their wickedness and their fathers' iniquity, asking him not to break his covenant, and resolving to wait for him.

l: false prophets, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 14
s: The prophets in the land tell the people they will not see sword or famine but will have assured peace. The LORD says he did not send, command, or speak to them, and that they prophesy lying visions, divination, and the deceit of their own heart. They will be consumed by sword and famine, and the prophet and priest are said to go about the land without knowledge.

l: sword, famine, and pestilence, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 14
s: The LORD declares he will consume the people by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence. The false prophets deny that sword and famine will come, but the LORD says those prophets will die by them. Jeremiah describes the slain with the sword in the field and those sick with famine in the city, and the people's corpses will lie unburied.

l: sins of the people, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 14
s: The people's iniquities and many rebellions are said to testify against them, and the LORD says he will remember their iniquity and punish their sins. He says he will pour their wickedness on them. The people themselves acknowledge their wickedness and the iniquity of their fathers, confessing they have sinned against the LORD.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 15
s: In Jeremiah 15 the LORD tells Jeremiah that even if Moses and Samuel interceded, he would not relent toward Judah's people, and he decrees death, sword, famine, and captivity for them, with the sword, dogs, birds, and animals as four destroyers, because of Manasseh's deeds in Jerusalem. He describes Jerusalem's loss of children, multiplied widows, and sudden terror, and says he is weary of showing compassion because the people rejected him and did not return. Jeremiah laments being a man of strife whom everyone curses, asks the LORD to avenge him, recalls delighting in the LORD's words, and complains that his pain is perpetual and that the LORD seems like a deceitful brook. The LORD responds that if Jeremiah returns and separates the precious from the vile he will be as the LORD's mouth, and promises to make him a fortified bronze wall and to deliver and redeem him from the wicked.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 15
s: The LORD declares that even Moses and Samuel could not turn his mind toward this people, and he decrees death, sword, famine, and captivity, with four kinds of destroyers, and says he is weary of showing compassion. He also answers Jeremiah, promising to strengthen him, make him a fortified bronze wall, and deliver and redeem him from the wicked, on condition that he return.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 15
s: Jeremiah is told not to expect the LORD to relent, and he laments that he is a man of strife and contention whom everyone curses though he has neither lent nor borrowed. He asks the LORD to remember and avenge him, recalls eating the LORD's words with joy, sitting alone out of indignation, and accuses the LORD of being like a failing brook. The LORD calls him to return, promising that he will be as his mouth and a bronze wall against opponents.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 15
s: Jerusalem is told that no one will pity it, mourn it, or ask after its welfare. Its people are tossed among the kingdoms because of what Manasseh, son of Hezekiah, did there, and the city suffers bereavement, widows more numerous than sand, and a destroyer at noonday.

l: people of Judah and Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 15
s: The people are cast out of the LORD's sight because they rejected him, went backward, and did not return from their ways. They are winnowed, bereaved of children, have their wealth plundered, are sent with their enemies into an unknown land, and their remnant is delivered to the sword.

l: judgment of death, sword, famine, and captivity, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 15
s: The LORD assigns each to its appointed fate: those for death to death, for the sword to the sword, for famine to famine, and for captivity to captivity. He appoints four kinds of destroyers: the sword to kill, dogs to tear, and the birds of the sky and animals of the earth to devour and destroy.

l: Jeremiah's suffering and complaint, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 15
s: Jeremiah cries woe that he was born a man of strife, cursed by all, and says he has suffered reproach for the LORD's sake and sat alone filled with indignation. He asks why his pain is perpetual and his wound incurable, and whether the LORD will be to him a deceitful brook. The LORD answers with a call to return and a promise of protection and rescue.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 16
s: The LORD commands the prophet, addressed as 'you', not to marry, have children, or attend houses of mourning or feasting in this place, as a sign that the children, parents, great and small will die by sword and famine, unlamented and unburied. The LORD declares he will end the voices of mirth, bridegroom and bride, and has withdrawn his peace, loving kindness and mercy from this people. When the people ask why, the prophet is to answer that they and their fathers forsook the LORD, served other gods, and that the present generation has done worse by following their stubborn evil hearts. Therefore the LORD will cast them into a land they and their fathers have not known, where they will serve other gods, and will repay their iniquity double for polluting his land. Yet he promises a future in which he is known as the one who brought Israel back from the north and all countries, restoring them to their land, and the speaker declares that the nations will come to the LORD and renounce their fathers' worthless gods.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 16
s: The LORD commands the prophet to forgo marriage, children, mourning and feasting, and announces that he has taken away his peace, loving kindness and tender mercies from this people. He sees all their ways, will repay their iniquity double, and will cast them into an unknown land. He also promises to bring Israel back from the north and all the countries and to make them know his hand, might and name.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 16
s: The text does not name him, but the one addressed as 'you' receives the LORD's word forbidding him to take a wife, have children, enter houses of mourning, or sit in houses of feasting. He is told to answer the people's questions about why the evil has come, and the speaker in verses 19-20 calls the LORD his strength, stronghold and refuge in the day of affliction.

l: people of Judah (this people), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 16
s: This people are told they will die grievous deaths, unlamented and unburied, by sword and famine, and that joy and wedding voices will cease in their days. They are charged with doing worse than their fathers by following their stubborn evil hearts and not listening, and they will be cast out to serve other gods in a foreign land and repaid double for their sin.

l: fathers (Israel's ancestors), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 16
s: Their fathers are said to have forsaken the LORD, walked after other gods, served and worshiped them, and not kept his law. The present generation is judged to have done even more evil than they. The LORD also says he gave the land to their fathers and will bring the people back into it, and the nations say their fathers inherited only lies and vanity.

l: plentiful land (land given to Israel), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 16
s: In this place, children, parents, great and small will die and go unburied, and the voices of mirth, bridegroom and bride will cease. The LORD calls it his land and inheritance, which the people polluted with the carcasses of detestable things and abominations, so they will be cast out of it.

l: Israel, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 16
s: The children of Israel are recalled as those the LORD brought up out of Egypt. A coming day is promised when he will instead be known as the one who brought them from the land of the north and all countries where he had driven them, and returned them to the land given to their fathers.

l: foreign land of exile, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 16
s: The LORD says he will cast the people into a land that neither they nor their fathers have known. There they will serve other gods day and night and receive no favor from him.

l: other gods, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 16
s: The fathers and their descendants walked after, served and worshiped other gods, which is the stated cause of the judgment. The people will serve them in exile, and the nations will eventually confess that such gods are vain and unprofitable, asking whether a man should make gods that are no gods.

l: judgment on Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 16
s: The LORD pronounces death by sword and famine, bodies left unburied as food for birds and animals, the end of mourning customs and joy, and expulsion to an unknown land. Their iniquity will be repaid double, and the LORD says he sees all their ways and nothing is hidden from him.

l: restoration of Israel (return from exile), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 16
s: The LORD promises that the days are coming when Israel's return from the north and all the countries of dispersion will replace the Exodus as the defining act of deliverance. He will send many fishermen and hunters to gather them from every mountain, hill and cleft of the rocks and bring them into the land he gave their fathers, though the recompense for their sin comes first.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 17
s: Chapter 17 opens with the LORD declaring that the sin of Judah is engraved on their hearts and altars, and that Judah will lose its treasures and heritage and serve enemies in an unknown land. It contrasts the cursed man who trusts in man, who is like a desert bush, with the blessed man who trusts in the LORD, who is like a tree planted by water. The LORD says he searches the heart and repays each person according to their deeds. The speaker prays for healing and refuge, complains that people mock him about the LORD's word, and asks that his persecutors be destroyed. The LORD then sends him to the gates of Jerusalem to tell the kings and people to keep the Sabbath holy and carry no burden, promising lasting blessing for obedience and a devouring, unquenched fire in the gates for disobedience.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 17
s: The LORD declares that Judah's sin is engraved on their hearts and altars and announces plunder and exile as consequences, with an anger-fire that burns forever. He curses the one who trusts in man, blesses the one who trusts in him, and says he searches the mind and tries the heart to repay each by his ways. He commissions the prophet to stand at Jerusalem's gates and proclaim the Sabbath command, promising enduring kings and offerings for obedience and an unquenched fire in the gates for disobedience.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 17
s: Judah's sin is described as written with an iron pen and diamond point on their hearts and altars, and even their children remember their altars and Asherah poles. The LORD says its wealth and high places will be plundered and that it will serve enemies in an unknown land. Its kings and people are addressed at the gates and told that Sabbath obedience would keep the city forever, while disobedience would bring fire.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 17
s: Jerusalem's gates are the setting where the prophet is told to proclaim the Sabbath command to the kings of Judah and all inhabitants. The LORD promises that if the Sabbath is kept, kings and princes on David's throne will enter and the city will remain forever, with people bringing offerings from surrounding regions. If not, he will kindle an unquenched fire in its gates that devours its palaces.

l: Sabbath day, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 17
s: The Sabbath day is to be made holy by bearing no burden out of houses or through Jerusalem's gates and doing no work, as the LORD commanded their fathers. The people did not listen but stiffened their necks. Keeping it brings lasting blessing for the city, while breaking it brings an unquenched fire.

l: Sin of Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 17
s: The sin of Judah is said to be written with a pen of iron and a diamond point, engraved on the tablet of their heart and the horns of their altars. It involves altars and Asherah poles on high hills, and results in plunder of their treasures and high places and loss of their heritage. It has kindled the LORD's anger like a fire that burns forever.

l: man who trusts in man, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 17
s: This man is cursed: he relies on the strength of flesh and his heart departs from the LORD. He is likened to a bush in the desert that does not see good come and lives in parched places and uninhabited salt land.

l: man who trusts in the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 17
s: This man is blessed, with his confidence in the LORD. He is likened to a tree planted by waters with roots by the river, unafraid when heat comes, green-leaved in drought, and never ceasing to yield fruit.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 17
s: The speaker asks the LORD to heal and save him, calling the LORD his praise and refuge in the day of evil. He says he has not hurried from shepherding after the LORD nor desired the woeful day, though people mock him by asking where the LORD's word is. He asks that his persecutors be disappointed and destroyed with double destruction, and he is then sent to stand in Jerusalem's gates to deliver the LORD's Sabbath message.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 18
s: The LORD tells Jeremiah to go to the potter's house, where he watches the potter remake a marred clay vessel into another one. The LORD explains that, like clay in the potter's hand, the house of Israel is in his hand, and that any nation he threatens with destruction may be spared if it turns from evil, while any nation he promises to build may lose that good if it disobeys. Jeremiah is to tell the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem to turn from their evil ways, but they answer that it is in vain and that they will follow their own plans. The LORD condemns Israel for forgetting him, burning incense to false gods, and leaving the ancient paths, and says he will scatter them before the enemy. Jeremiah's opponents plot to strike him with the tongue and ignore his words, and Jeremiah prays that the LORD hear him, remember that he spoke good for them, and deal with them in anger without forgiving their sin.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 18
s: Jeremiah is told by the LORD to go down to the potter's house, where he sees the potter remake a marred vessel, and he receives the LORD's word explaining it. He is to speak the LORD's warning to Judah and Jerusalem, and he becomes the target of a plot against him. He prays that the LORD listen to him, recalls that he once stood before the LORD to speak good for them, and asks that their children and men suffer and that their sin not be forgiven.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 18
s: The LORD sends Jeremiah to the potter's house and uses the potter's work to say that Israel is in his hand as clay is in the potter's. He declares that he will relent from evil or good toward a nation depending on its response, warns Judah that he is framing evil against them, and says he will scatter them like an east wind and show them his back in their calamity. Jeremiah calls on him to hear and to deal with those who plot against him, and says the LORD knows all their counsel to kill him.

l: potter (potter's house), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 18
s: The potter is seen by Jeremiah at his house working on the wheels. When the vessel he is making is marred in his hand, he makes it again into another vessel as seems good to him, which the LORD uses as an image of his own right over Israel.

l: clay vessel (potter's vessel), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 18
s: The vessel made of clay is marred in the potter's hand, and the potter makes it again into another vessel as seems good to him. It serves as the image of the house of Israel in the LORD's hand.

l: Israel, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 18
s: The house of Israel is told by the LORD that it is in his hand as the clay is in the potter's hand. It is also called the virgin of Israel, which has done a very horrible thing, and the LORD says his people have forgotten him, burned incense to false gods, and stumbled from the ancient paths into byways, so that their land will become an astonishment and a perpetual hissing.

l: men of Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 18
s: The men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem are to be told that the LORD frames evil and devises a plan against them, and that they should each return from their evil way and amend their doings. They reply that it is in vain and that they will walk after their own plans and follow the stubbornness of their evil hearts.

l: nation (any nation spoken of by the LORD), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 18
s: The LORD says that when he speaks of plucking up, breaking down, and destroying a nation or kingdom, he will repent of the evil he planned if that nation turns from its evil. When he speaks of building and planting a nation, he will repent of the good he promised if it does evil and does not obey his voice.

l: Jeremiah's opponents, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 18
s: Jeremiah's opponents say "Come!" and propose devising plans against him, trusting that the law, counsel, and the word will not perish from the priest, the wise, and the prophet. They plan to strike him with the tongue and ignore his words, and Jeremiah says they have dug a pit for his soul and hidden snares for his feet, wanting to kill him.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 19
s: The LORD commands Jeremiah to buy a potter's earthen container and take elders of the people and of the priests to the valley of the son of Hinnom, by the entry of the gate Harsith. There Jeremiah is to proclaim judgment on the kings of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem for forsaking the LORD, burning incense to other gods, shedding innocent blood, and burning their children to Baal. The LORD declares that the place will be renamed the valley of Slaughter, that Judah's counsel will be made void, that people will die by the sword and be food for birds and animals, and that the city will become an astonishment and a hissing, with siege-time cannibalism. Jeremiah is to break the container before the men with him as a sign that the LORD will break the people and city beyond repair, making Jerusalem's houses like Topheth. Jeremiah then returns from Topheth, stands in the court of the LORD's house, and tells all the people that the LORD will bring all the pronounced evil on the city and its towns because they have stiffened their necks and refused to hear.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 19
s: The LORD commands Jeremiah to buy a potter's container, go to the valley of the son of Hinnom, and proclaim judgment on Judah and Jerusalem. He declares that he did not command, speak of, or conceive the child burning to Baal, and he vows to bring evil on the place, void Judah's counsel, and break the people and city like a potter's vessel.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 19
s: Jeremiah is sent to buy a potter's container, take elders to the valley of the son of Hinnom, proclaim the LORD's words, and break the container before the men with him. He then returns from Topheth, stands in the court of the LORD's house, and repeats to all the people that the LORD will bring the pronounced evil on the city.

l: potter’s earthen container (Jeremiah's purchase), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 19
s: The LORD tells Jeremiah to buy it and take it to the valley of the son of Hinnom. Jeremiah is to break it in the sight of the men with him, as a sign that the LORD will break this people and city so that it cannot be made whole again.

l: valley of the son of Hinnom, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 19
s: It is the place by the entry of the gate Harsith where Jeremiah is sent to proclaim the LORD's words. The LORD says it will no more be called by that name or Topheth, but 'The valley of Slaughter'.

l: Topheth, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 19
s: Topheth is a place where the LORD says they will bury until there is no place left to bury. He will make Jerusalem as Topheth, and the defiled houses of Jerusalem and of the kings of Judah will be like the place of Topheth. Jeremiah comes from Topheth, where the LORD had sent him to prophesy.

l: inhabitants of Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 19
s: Along with the kings of Judah, they are addressed as having forsaken the LORD, defiled the place, burned incense to unknown gods, and filled it with innocent blood. The LORD says they will fall by the sword, be given as food to birds and animals, and eat the flesh of their children and friends in the siege.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 19
s: The LORD says he will make this city an astonishment and a hissing, and that all who pass by will be astonished and hiss at its plagues.
