He will break it like a potter's vessel, make it like Topheth, and bring on it and all its towns all the evil he has pronounced because of their stiff-necked refusal to hear.

l: child sacrifice, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 19
s: The LORD charges that they built high places of Baal to burn their children in the fire as burnt offerings, which he did not command, speak, or even conceive. It is named among the reasons for the coming judgment on the place.

l: siege and cannibalism judgment, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 19
s: The LORD says he will cause the people to eat the flesh of their sons and daughters, and each to eat the flesh of his friend, during the siege and the distress inflicted by their enemies and those seeking their lives. It is part of the judgment announced against Judah and Jerusalem.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 20
s: Pashhur, the priest and chief officer in the LORD's house, hears Jeremiah prophesying, strikes him, and puts him in the stocks at the upper gate of Benjamin. When released the next day, Jeremiah renames Pashhur Magormissabib and declares that the LORD will give Judah and its treasures to the king of Babylon, and that Pashhur and his household will die in Babylonian captivity. Jeremiah then laments that the LORD has overpowered him, that he is mocked all day, and that he cannot hold back the LORD's word, which burns in his bones. He recounts the plots of his familiar friends, expresses confidence that the LORD will make his persecutors stumble, and calls on the LORD to avenge him. The chapter closes with a call to praise the LORD, followed by Jeremiah cursing the day of his birth and asking why he came out of the womb to see sorrow and shame.

l: Pashhur, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 20
s: Pashhur, son of Immer the priest and chief officer in the LORD's house, heard Jeremiah prophesying, struck him, and put him in the stocks at the upper gate of Benjamin. The next day he released Jeremiah, who renamed him Magormissabib and foretold that he would become a terror to himself and his friends. Pashhur and his household were told they would go into captivity in Babylon, where he would die and be buried, having prophesied falsely to his friends.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 20
s: Jeremiah was struck and put in the stocks by Pashhur after prophesying, and after his release he pronounced judgment on Pashhur in the LORD's name. He complains that he is a laughingstock and that the LORD's word has become a reproach, yet he cannot stay silent because the word burns in his bones. He trusts the LORD is with him against his enemies, but ends by cursing the day of his birth and asking why he was born to see sorrow and shame.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 20
s: The LORD declares through Jeremiah that Pashhur will be a terror to himself and his friends and that Judah and its treasures will be given to the king of Babylon. Jeremiah says the LORD persuaded him and prevailed over him, and describes him as an awesome mighty one who is with him, who tests the righteous, sees the heart and mind, and delivers the needy from evildoers.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 20
s: The LORD says he will give all Judah into the hand of the king of Babylon, who will carry its people captive to Babylon and kill them with the sword. The riches, gains, precious things, and treasures of the kings of Judah will also be given to their enemies and carried off to Babylon.

l: king of Babylon, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 20
s: The LORD says he will give all Judah into the king of Babylon's hand. The king will carry the people captive to Babylon and kill them with the sword.

l: Babylon, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 20
s: Babylon is named as the place to which Judah's people and treasures will be carried as captives and spoil. Pashhur, his household, and his friends will go there, and Pashhur will die and be buried there.

l: persecutors (of Jeremiah), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 20
s: Jeremiah's familiar friends defame him, saying "Terror on every side! Denounce, and we will denounce him," and watch for his fall hoping to prevail and take revenge. Jeremiah asserts that the LORD will make his persecutors stumble, disappoint them, and bring them everlasting dishonor, and he asks to see the LORD's vengeance on them.

l: Jeremiah's prophecy of Babylonian conquest, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 20
s: Jeremiah declares in the LORD's name that all Judah will be given to the king of Babylon, with its people killed or taken captive and its treasures carried off to Babylon. He applies it personally to Pashhur, who will die in Babylon with his household and friends. The prophecy is what provoked Pashhur to put Jeremiah in the stocks.

l: Jeremiah's lament, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 20
s: Jeremiah laments that the LORD has overpowered him, that he is mocked daily, and that his proclamations of violence and destruction bring reproach. He says he cannot keep silent because the LORD's word burns like fire in his bones. The lament closes with curses on the day of his birth and on the man who announced it, and the question of why he came from the womb to see labor, sorrow, and shame.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 21
s: King Zedekiah sends Pashhur son of Malchijah and Zephaniah son of Maaseiah to ask Jeremiah to inquire of the LORD, hoping the LORD will make Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon withdraw. Jeremiah answers that the LORD himself will fight against Jerusalem, turn back its defenders' weapons, and strike the city with pestilence. Afterward Zedekiah, his servants, and the survivors will be delivered into Nebuchadnezzar's hand and killed without mercy. The people are offered the way of life, which is to go out to the Chaldeans, or the way of death, which is to stay in the city. The LORD also tells the House of David to execute justice or face a fire of wrath, and he declares he is against the city's overconfident inhabitants.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 21
s: Jeremiah is asked by Zedekiah, through Pashhur and Zephaniah, to inquire of the LORD about Nebuchadnezzar's war. He delivers the LORD's answer of judgment to Zedekiah, the people, and the House of David, rather than the hoped-for deliverance.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 21
s: The LORD declares that he himself will fight against Jerusalem with an outstretched hand and a strong arm, in anger and wrath. He will turn back the defenders' weapons, send pestilence, and give the city and Zedekiah into Nebuchadnezzar's hand. He sets before the people the way of life and the way of death, calls the House of David to execute justice, and promises to punish according to the fruit of their doings.

l: Zedekiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 21
s: Zedekiah sends Pashhur and Zephaniah to ask Jeremiah to inquire of the LORD, hoping the LORD will deal with them according to his wondrous works so that Nebuchadnezzar withdraws. The answer is that he, his servants, and the surviving people will be delivered into Nebuchadnezzar's hand and struck with the sword without pity or mercy.

l: Nebuchadnezzar, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 21
s: Nebuchadnezzar is making war against Zedekiah and the city, and his forces besiege it. The LORD says he will give Zedekiah, his servants, and the survivors into Nebuchadnezzar's hand, and that Nebuchadnezzar will burn the city with fire and strike them without sparing, pity, or mercy.

l: Chaldeans, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 21
s: The Chaldeans besiege the city from outside the walls. The LORD says he will turn the defenders' weapons back and gather them into the middle of the city. Anyone who goes out and passes over to the Chaldeans will live and escape with his life.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 21
s: The LORD has set his face against the city for evil and not for good. Its inhabitants, man and animal, will be struck by a great pestilence, and the city will be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, who will burn it with fire. The LORD also says he will kindle a fire in its forest that devours all around it.

l: House of David, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 21
s: The house of the king of Judah is told to execute justice in the morning and deliver the robbed from the hand of the oppressor. Otherwise the LORD's wrath will go out like an unquenchable fire because of the evil of their doings. The LORD says he will punish them according to the fruit of their doings.

l: people of the city (Zedekiah's people), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 21
s: The people are told that those who remain in the city will die by the sword, famine, and pestilence. Those who go out to the besieging Chaldeans will live. Those left after the pestilence will be delivered into Nebuchadnezzar's hand and struck down without mercy.

l: siege of Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 21
s: Nebuchadnezzar makes war against Judah, and the Chaldeans besiege the city outside the walls. Zedekiah hopes the LORD will cause the attackers to withdraw. The LORD instead says he will turn the defenders' weapons back, fight against the city himself, and give it into Babylon's hand to be burned.

l: pestilence, sword, and famine, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 21
s: The LORD says he will strike the inhabitants of the city, both man and animal, with a great pestilence. Those who remain in the city are said to die by the sword, famine, and pestilence. Survivors of these are to be delivered into Nebuchadnezzar's hand.

l: way of life and the way of death, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 21
s: The LORD sets these two ways before the people. The way of death is to remain in the city and die by sword, famine, and pestilence. The way of life is to go out and pass over to the besieging Chaldeans, escaping with one's life.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 22
s: The LORD sends a message to the house of the king of Judah, calling it to execute justice and righteousness and warning that disobedience will make the house a desolation, with nations later explaining the ruin as punishment for abandoning the covenant. The chapter then addresses specific kings: Shallum son of Josiah will die in captivity and never return, and Jehoiakim son of Josiah is condemned for building his house by injustice and unpaid labor, in contrast to his father who did justice and judged the cause of the poor. Jehoiakim is told he will be buried like a donkey and cast out beyond Jerusalem's gates. Coniah son of Jehoiakim is declared to be given into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and cast out with his mother to a foreign land where he will die. The LORD finally commands that Coniah be recorded as childless, with none of his offspring prospering on David's throne.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 22
s: The LORD sends a word to the house of the king of Judah, demanding justice and righteousness and swearing by himself that disobedience will make the house a desolation. He pronounces woe on unjust building, announces the fates of Shallum, Jehoiakim, and Coniah, and says he would pluck Coniah away even if he were the signet on his right hand.

l: king of Judah (house of the king of Judah), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 22
s: The king of Judah, who sits on David's throne, is told to hear the LORD's word along with his servants and people. If they do justice, kings will keep entering the gates on chariots and horses; if not, the house will become a desolation.

l: house of the king of Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 22
s: The house of the king of Judah is called Gilead and the head of Lebanon to the LORD, yet he will make it a wilderness. Destroyers will cut down its choice cedars and burn them, and passing nations will be told it fell because they abandoned the LORD's covenant and served other gods.

l: Shallum, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 22
s: Shallum, son of Josiah, reigned instead of his father and went out of this place. The LORD says he will never return, will die where he was led captive, and will not see the land again; people are told to weep for him rather than for the dead.

l: Jehoiakim, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 22
s: Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, is condemned for building a wide house with cedar and red paint using his neighbor's unpaid labor, and for covetousness, shedding innocent blood, oppression, and violence. He is told no one will lament him and that he will be buried like a donkey, drawn and cast out beyond Jerusalem's gates.

l: Coniah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 22
s: Coniah, son of Jehoiakim, is declared to be handed over to those seeking his life, including Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and the Chaldeans. He and his mother will be cast into a foreign land to die and never return, and he is to be recorded as childless, with none of his offspring prospering on David's throne.

l: justice and righteousness, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 22
s: The LORD commands the king's house to execute justice and righteousness, deliver the robbed from the oppressor, and not wrong foreigners, the fatherless, or widows. Josiah is cited as having done justice and righteousness, so that it was well with him, and judging the cause of the poor and needy is described as knowing the LORD.

l: unjust house-building, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 22
s: The LORD pronounces woe on one who builds his house by unrighteousness and his rooms by injustice, using his neighbor's service without wages. It is exemplified by a wide house with cedar ceiling painted red, and the LORD asks whether excelling in cedar justifies reigning.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 23
s: In Jeremiah 23 the LORD pronounces woe on the shepherds who have scattered and driven away his flock, and promises to gather the remnant, set up faithful shepherds, and raise a righteous Branch for David who will reign wisely and be called 'The LORD our righteousness.' The chapter then turns to the prophets and priests of Samaria and Jerusalem, whom the LORD accuses of profanity, adultery, lies, and encouraging evildoers, likening Jerusalem to Sodom and Gomorrah and promising them wormwood and poisoned water. The LORD warns the people not to heed prophets who speak visions of their own hearts and promise peace, since they were not sent and have not stood in his council. He declares that he sees everywhere, fills heaven and earth, and is against those who tell lying dreams and steal or invent his words, contrasting straw with wheat and likening his word to fire and a hammer. The chapter ends with a ban on the phrase 'the message from the LORD', because people have perverted the words of the living God, and the LORD threatens to forget and cast off those who use it, bringing everlasting reproach and shame.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 23
s: The LORD pronounces woe on the shepherds who scattered his flock and promises to gather the remnant, set up new shepherds, and raise a righteous Branch for David. He declares himself against prophets who prophesy lies, saying he did not send them, and affirms that he fills heaven and earth and sees all hidden places. He ends by threatening to utterly forget and cast off those who misuse 'the message from the LORD', bringing everlasting reproach.

l: shepherds (of the LORD's flock), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 23
s: The shepherds are accused of destroying and scattering the LORD's flock, driving them away and not visiting them, and the LORD says he will visit on them the evil of their doings. He promises to set up other shepherds over the flock who will feed them so that none will be afraid, dismayed, or lacking.

l: flock (the LORD's people), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 23
s: The flock has been scattered and driven into many countries by its shepherds. The LORD promises to gather the remnant, bring them back to their folds, and make them fruitful and multiply. They are told not to listen to the prophets who give them vain visions, and they are warned against perverting the LORD's words.

l: Israel, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 23
s: Israel is promised that it will dwell safely in the days of the righteous Branch, and that people will no longer remember the exodus from Egypt but instead the LORD who led the offspring of Israel out of the north country and all countries where he had driven them, so they will dwell in their own land. The prophets of Samaria are said to have prophesied by Baal and caused Israel to err.

l: righteous Branch (of David), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 23
s: The LORD promises to raise a righteous Branch to David who will reign as king, deal wisely, and execute justice and righteousness in the land. In his days Judah will be saved and Israel will dwell safely, and he will be called 'The LORD our righteousness.'

l: prophets, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 23
s: The prophets of Samaria and Jerusalem are condemned: those in Samaria prophesied by Baal, and those in Jerusalem commit adultery, walk in lies, strengthen evildoers, and have become like Sodom and Gomorrah. The LORD says he did not send them, that they have not stood in his council, and that he is against them for stealing his words and prophesying lying dreams; he will feed them wormwood and poisoned water.

l: false dreams, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 23
s: The prophets claim 'I had a dream!' and tell lying dreams in the LORD's name, which the LORD says come from the deceit of their own hearts. He says these dreams aim to make his people forget his name as their fathers did because of Baal, that they cause the people to err, and that they profit the people not at all.

l: the LORD's word, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 23
s: The LORD contrasts a mere dream with his word as straw is to wheat, and says his word is like fire and like a hammer that breaks rock in pieces. A prophet who has his word is to speak it faithfully, while those who steal it or say 'He says' are condemned.

l: the message from the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 23
s: The phrase 'the message from the LORD' is forbidden because every man's own word has become his message, perverting the words of the living God. The LORD says that anyone who uses the phrase will be punished along with his household, and that those who persist will be forgotten and cast off from his presence.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 24
s: The LORD shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs set before the LORD's temple, after Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has carried Jeconiah, the princes of Judah, and the craftsmen and smiths captive to Babylon. One basket holds very good, first-ripe figs and the other holds figs so bad they cannot be eaten. The LORD explains that the good figs stand for the captives of Judah sent to the land of the Chaldeans, whom he will regard as good, bring back to the land, build and plant, and give a heart to know him. The bad figs stand for Zedekiah king of Judah, his princes, the remnant of Jerusalem, and those living in Egypt, whom the LORD will give up to be scattered among the kingdoms as a reproach, proverb, taunt, and curse. He will send sword, famine, and pestilence among them until they are consumed from the land he gave to them and their fathers.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 24
s: The LORD shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs and asks him what he sees, then explains that the good figs represent the captives of Judah, whom he will watch over for good, return to the land, and give a heart to know him. He declares that he will give up Zedekiah, his princes, the remnant of Jerusalem, and those in Egypt, sending sword, famine, and pestilence until they are consumed from the land.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 24
s: Jeremiah is shown two baskets of figs before the LORD's temple and, when asked what he sees, answers that the good figs are very good and the bad figs are so bad they cannot be eaten. He then receives the LORD's word interpreting the vision.

l: good figs, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 24
s: The good figs are in one basket, very good like first-ripe figs. The LORD says they represent the captives of Judah sent to the land of the Chaldeans, whom he regards as good.

l: bad figs, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 24
s: The bad figs are in the other basket and are so bad that they cannot be eaten. The LORD says they represent Zedekiah, his princes, the remnant of Jerusalem, and those dwelling in Egypt, who will be given up to judgment.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 24
s: Judah's king Jeconiah, its princes, and its craftsmen and smiths have been carried captive to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar. The LORD distinguishes between Judah's captives, who are regarded as good, and Zedekiah its king with his princes, who are regarded as bad.

l: captives of Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 24
s: The captives of Judah, sent out of this place into the land of the Chaldeans, are likened to the good figs and regarded as good. The LORD promises to set his eyes on them for good, bring them back to the land, build and plant them, and give them a heart to know him, so that they become his people and return to him with their whole heart.

l: Zedekiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 24
s: Zedekiah, king of Judah, is likened to the bad figs. The LORD says he will give up Zedekiah and his princes to be tossed among all the kingdoms of the earth as a reproach, proverb, taunt, and curse.

l: remnant of Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 24
s: The remnant of Jerusalem who remain in the land is likened to the bad figs and named among those the LORD will give up. They face sword, famine, and pestilence, and being driven out among the kingdoms until they are consumed from the land.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 25
s: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, Jeremiah tells all Judah and Jerusalem that for twenty-three years the LORD's word and his prophets have called them to turn from evil and other gods, but they have not listened. Therefore the LORD will bring the families of the north and Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, his servant, against Judah and the surrounding nations, who will serve Babylon seventy years. After seventy years the LORD will punish Babylon and make the land of the Chaldeans desolate forever. Jeremiah is told to take the cup of the wine of wrath and make all the nations drink it, from Jerusalem and Egypt to the kings of the north, with the king of Sheshach drinking last. The chapter ends with the LORD roaring in judgment against all the inhabitants of the earth, the slain lying unburied, and the shepherds wailing as their pasture is destroyed.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 25
s: The LORD says he has sent his prophets persistently to call Judah to repent, and because they did not listen he will bring the families of the north and Nebuchadnezzar against the land and the surrounding nations. He gives Jeremiah the cup of wrath for all the nations, declares he will punish Babylon after seventy years, and roars from on high in judgment on all flesh.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 25
s: Jeremiah speaks to all Judah and Jerusalem in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, saying the LORD's word has come to him for twenty-three years and that he has spoken early and often without being heeded. He takes the cup from the LORD's hand and makes the nations drink it, then is told to prophesy the LORD's roaring judgment against them all.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 25
s: Judah is told it has not listened to the LORD or his prophets, and that it will become a desolation along with the surrounding nations. Its cities, kings and princes are among those made to drink the cup, becoming a desolation, an astonishment, a hissing and a curse.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 25
s: Its inhabitants are addressed by Jeremiah and it is the first to drink the cup of wrath. The LORD says he begins to work evil at the city called by his name, and asks whether the nations should then go unpunished.

l: Nebuchadnezzar, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 25
s: Nebuchadnezzar is king of Babylon, whose first year matches Jehoiakim's fourth. The LORD calls him "my servant" and says he will send him with the families of the north against Judah, its inhabitants and the surrounding nations.

l: Babylon, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 25
s: Babylon's king, Nebuchadnezzar, is the instrument of the LORD's judgment, and the nations will serve him seventy years. When the seventy years are complete, the LORD will punish the king of Babylon and his nation for their iniquity and make the land of the Chaldeans desolate forever, as written against it in this book.

l: cup of the wine of wrath, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 25
s: The LORD gives Jeremiah this cup to make all the nations drink, causing them to reel, be insane and fall because of the sword he will send. Those who refuse are told they will surely drink, and the king of Sheshach is named to drink after the others.

l: nations (under Nebuchadnezzar's yoke), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 25
s: The nations, listed from Egypt, Uz, the Philistine cities, Edom, Moab and Ammon to Tyre, Sidon, Arabia, Elam, the Medes and the kings of the north, are all made to drink the cup. They will serve Babylon seventy years and face the sword, with the slain left unlamented and unburied across the earth.

l: divine judgment on the nations, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 25
s: The LORD declares he has a controversy with the nations and will enter into judgment with all flesh, giving the wicked to the sword. Evil will go out from nation to nation, a great storm will rise, and the slain will lie from one end of the earth to the other, while the shepherds and leaders of the flock find no escape.

l: Judah's disobedience, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 25
s: For twenty-three years Judah did not listen to Jeremiah or the prophets calling it to return from evil, dwell in the land, and stop following other gods. It provoked the LORD to anger with the work of its hands to its own hurt, which is the stated reason for the coming judgment.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 26
s: In the early reign of Jehoiakim of Judah, the LORD commands Jeremiah to stand in the LORD's house and warn the people that, unless they listen, the house will become like Shiloh and the city a curse to all nations. The priests, prophets, and people seize Jeremiah and demand his death, but the princes of Judah come up from the king's house and hear the case. Jeremiah urges them to amend their ways and warns that killing him would bring innocent blood on them, and the princes and people rule that he is not worthy of death. Elders cite Micah the Morashtite, who prophesied against Zion under Hezekiah and was not killed, while Jehoiakim had Uriah son of Shemaiah killed after retrieving him from Egypt. Ahikam son of Shaphan protects Jeremiah from being handed over to the people.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 26
s: Jeremiah speaks the LORD's words of warning in the LORD's house and is seized by the priests, prophets, and people, who say he must die. He defends himself before the princes, urging repentance and warning of innocent blood, and is acquitted, with Ahikam son of Shaphan ensuring he is not given to the people.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 26
s: The LORD commands Jeremiah to speak every word to the cities of Judah, hoping they will listen and turn so that he may relent from the disaster he intends. He threatens to make the house like Shiloh and the city a curse to all nations if they will not listen to his law and his prophets.

l: Jehoiakim, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 26
s: Jehoiakim is king of Judah, the son of Josiah, at the time of this word from the LORD. He sought to kill Uriah for prophesying like Jeremiah, sent Elnathan son of Achbor and others to fetch him from Egypt, and killed him with the sword.

l: the LORD’s house, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 26
s: The LORD's house is where Jeremiah is told to stand and speak to those who come to worship, and where the crowd seizes him. The LORD warns it will become like Shiloh, and the princes sit in the entry of its new gate to hear the case.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 26
s: Jerusalem is the city the LORD threatens to make a curse to all the nations and to leave desolate without inhabitant. The elders recall Micah's saying that it would become heaps.

l: priests, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 26
s: The priests, with the prophets and people, seize Jeremiah and say he shall surely die for prophesying against the house and city. They tell the princes and people he is worthy of death, but the princes and people reject their claim.

l: prophets, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 26
s: The prophets join the priests and people in seizing Jeremiah and declaring him worthy of death for prophesying against the city. The princes and people reject this verdict. The LORD also speaks of his servants the prophets whom he sent persistently, and whom the people did not heed.

l: people of Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 26
s: The people hear Jeremiah, crowd around him, and join in seizing him and demanding his death. After the princes hear the case, the people side with them in declaring he is not worthy of death because he spoke in the LORD's name, and Ahikam keeps him from being given into their hands.

l: princes of Judah and Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 26
s: The princes come up from the king's house and sit in the entry of the new gate to hear the accusation against Jeremiah. They and the people rule that he is not worthy of death because he has spoken in the name of the LORD.

l: Uriah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 26
s: Uriah son of Shemaiah of Kiriath Jearim prophesied in the LORD's name against the city and land in words like Jeremiah's. When Jehoiakim sought to kill him he fled to Egypt, but he was brought back and killed with the sword, and his body was cast into the graves of the common people.

l: Jeremiah's prophecy of destruction, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 26
s: Jeremiah's message says that if the people will not listen to the LORD's law and prophets, the house will become like Shiloh and the city a curse to all nations. It provokes the demand for his death, but it is offered conditionally, with the chance that the LORD will relent if they amend their ways, and the elders compare it to Micah's similar prophecy.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 27
s: In Jeremiah 27, the LORD tells Jeremiah to make bonds and bars, wear them on his neck, and send word to the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon through their messengers in Jerusalem. The message is that the LORD, creator of the earth, has given all these lands and the animals to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, whom all nations will serve until his own land's time comes. Nations that refuse to put their necks under Babylon's yoke will be punished with sword, famine, and pestilence, while those that submit will remain in their land. Jeremiah repeats this to Zedekiah king of Judah, and to the priests and people, warning them not to listen to prophets, diviners, and others who say they will not serve Babylon or that the temple vessels will soon return. The LORD says the remaining vessels in the temple, the king's house, and Jerusalem will also be carried to Babylon, where they will stay until the LORD visits them and restores them to Jerusalem.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 27
s: The LORD commands Jeremiah to make bonds and bars and send a message to the surrounding kings, declaring that he made the earth and gives it to whom he chooses. He has given the lands to Nebuchadnezzar, will punish nations that refuse to serve him, denies having sent the prophets who say otherwise, and promises that the vessels carried to Babylon will one day be brought back and restored.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 27
s: Jeremiah is told by the LORD to make bonds and bars, put them on his neck, and send word to the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon. He then speaks to Zedekiah, and to the priests and people, urging them to serve the king of Babylon and live, and to ignore prophets who say otherwise.

l: Nebuchadnezzar, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 27
s: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon is called the LORD's servant, to whom the LORD has given all these lands and the animals of the field. All nations will serve him, his son, and his son's son until the time of his own land comes, and any nation refusing his yoke will be punished until consumed by his hand.

l: Zedekiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 27
s: Zedekiah king of Judah is addressed by Jeremiah, who tells him to bring his people's necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, serve him, and live. He is asked why he and his people should die by sword, famine, and pestilence, and is warned not to heed prophets who say they will not serve Babylon.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 27
s: Judah's king Zedekiah and its people are told to submit to Babylon to avoid sword, famine, and pestilence. The text recalls that Nebuchadnezzar earlier carried away Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and Judah's and Jerusalem's nobles to Babylon.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 27
s: Jerusalem is where the messengers of the foreign kings come to Zedekiah, and Jeremiah warns that the city could become a desolation if it does not serve Babylon. The vessels still left in the city will be carried to Babylon, but the LORD promises to restore them to this place.
